title: Beyond Light Cones: State Preparation Complexity in Quantum Spin Glasses
authors: Omar Al-Ghattas, David Gamarnik, Bobak T Kiani
abstract: We introduce a method for studying state preparation complexity in dense quantum $p$-spin Hamiltonians on $n$ qubits, going beyond bounds based only on circuit lightcones. The key input is the class's effective profile complexity, which is derived from the metric entropy of its Pauli profiles. These profiles record expectations of all Pauli operators supported on exactly $p$ qubits. Classes with uniformly bounded quadratic effective profile complexity remain separated from the ground-state energy by a positive multiple of $\sqrt n$ for sufficiently large fixed $p$. At subquadratic effective profile complexity, the class cannot outperform a suitable benchmark class at leading order, with product states providing a universal benchmark. The proof combines an adaptation of a nonsymmetric quantum de Finetti theorem of Berta et al. (arXiv:1810.12197) with Gaussian process entropy bounds.   Applying this framework, we show that attaining near-ground-state energy requires $Ω(n^2/\log n)$ one- and two-qubit gates, even with arbitrary discardable ancillas. We also obtain depth-width tradeoffs, entanglement-depth and matrix product state bond-dimension lower bounds, and obstructions for both orientations at every fixed level of Parham's magic hierarchy (arXiv:2504.19966), with total circuit width $O(n)$. In first-level reverse magic, a shallow circuit is followed by an unrestricted Clifford circuit. The latter can spread local observables across the system, preventing a direct application of small-lightcone bounds. For this first-level class, our bounds also allow arbitrarily many clean ancillas at fixed shallow-circuit depth. A sharper benchmark shows that Clifford+$T$ circuits with $o(n)$ $T$-gates have no leading-order energy advantage over product stabilizer states, even with unrestricted Clifford operations and arbitrary discardable ancillas.
summary: This work develops a sophisticated framework to quantify how hard it is to prepare quantum states close to the ground state of quantum spin glasses. By analyzing the 'profile complexity' of the state class, the authors derive lower bounds on the required quantum circuit resources, showing that simple local constraints are insufficient to capture the true preparation difficulty.
main_problem: The paper studies the state preparation complexity of quantum states in dense quantum $p$-spin Hamiltonians, aiming to derive energy lower bounds that surpass those based solely on circuit lightcones.
main_result: It establishes that attaining near-ground-state energy requires $\Omega(n^2 / \log n)$ one- and two-qubit gates, and provides lower bounds for various circuit resource trade-offs.
method: The core method involves using the effective profile complexity, derived from the metric entropy of Pauli profiles, combined with an adaptation of a nonsymmetric quantum de Finetti theorem.
model_or_system: The focus is on dense quantum $p$-spin Hamiltonians acting on $n$ qubits, which model quantum spin glasses. The analysis compares the energy achievable by a restricted state class to a benchmark class.
key_observables: Profile complexity, ground-state energy separation ($\Delta$), circuit gate counts (one- and two-qubit gates), entanglement depth, and MPS bond dimension.
important_parameters: The fixed parameter $p$ (number of qubits involved in interactions), the system size $n$, and the profile complexity regime (e.g., subquadratic vs. quadratic).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a suitable benchmark class $	ext{Bn}$ and relies on adapting advanced theorems like the nonsymmetric quantum de Finetti theorem.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the profile complexity principle, applies it to various structured state classes (including those related to the magic hierarchy), and derives quantitative bounds on resource requirements.
why_interesting: The techniques developed—using profile complexity and metric entropy to bound energy gaps—provide powerful, non-local tools for characterizing the computational difficulty of preparing ground states in complex, disordered quantum systems.
